name: Berberine
lead: Berberine is a yellow quaternary ammonium alkaloid of the benzylisoquinoline class found in the roots, bark and stems of plants such as barberry (Berberis vulgaris), tree turmeric, Oregon grape, goldenseal and Chinese goldthread.[1] Plants containing it have a long history in traditional medicine, and extracts are sold as dietary supplements. Wikipedia notes that, outside China where it is an over-the-counter drug for diarrhea, berberine is not approved as a prescription medicine in any country.[1]

In appearance and body-composition communities it is used for appetite, blood sugar and nutrient-partitioning goals and is nicknamed "nature's metformin" because it activates the same energy-sensing enzyme, AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), that metformin engages.[2][5] An umbrella review of 11 meta-analyses of randomized trials reported that berberine was associated with improvements in blood glucose, insulin resistance, lipids, body parameters and inflammatory markers compared with controls, while noting that the methodological quality of the meta-analyses needed improvement.[3]

The most common adverse effects are gastrointestinal. Berberine inhibits the drug-metabolising enzyme CYP3A4 and has been reported to raise concentrations of ciclosporin and midazolam, and the US FDA issued warning letters to supplement makers about berberine marketing claims between 2020 and 2022.[1]

paras: Berberine is taken by people interested in fat loss and body recomposition, usually to influence blood sugar, appetite or what is called nutrient partitioning. A systematic review specifically on berberine and weight loss has been published, and the umbrella review lists body weight and composition among the outcomes assessed in meta-analyses.[3][4]

On T Nation, lifters describe using it during cuts or bulks, sometimes together with cinnamon extract, apple cider vinegar or insulin-sensitising drugs. Some posters report taking it because of a poor diet or elevated HbA1c, while one reports that it suppressed hunger with severe gastrointestinal effects.[11][12][13][14]

Traditional use includes treating infections and diarrhea. In China the compound is approved over the counter for diarrhea, and its package insert contraindicates it in people with hemolytic anemia or G6PD deficiency.[1] Most modern clinical research concerns type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia and metabolic syndrome.[3][6][7]

A 2008 pilot randomized trial in adults with type 2 diabetes found that 0.5 g of berberine three times daily for three months lowered HbA1c, fasting glucose and triglycerides, with a glucose-lowering effect comparable to metformin in the 36-person comparison; a second uncontrolled arm of 48 adults with poorly controlled diabetes also showed reductions in HbA1c and insulin resistance.[8]

Meta-analyses of randomized trials in type 2 diabetes report significant reductions in fasting glucose, HbA1c and postprandial glucose, with some analyses also reporting effects on lipids, insulin resistance and body mass index.[6][7][9] A 2014 meta-analysis addressed diabetes, hyperlipidemia and hypertension, and a 2023 analysis examined dyslipidemia including sex-specific effects.[10][15] The umbrella review summarises the evidence as favourable for glucose and lipids and cautions that the underlying trials are often small and of uneven quality.[3]

A systematic review published in 2020 assessed berberine for weight loss and obesity prevention.[4] More recent randomized trials include a 2025 phase II trial of a berberine ursodeoxycholate salt in type 2 diabetes, a 2023 pilot trial in prediabetes, a trial combining berberine with probiotics (the PREMOTE study) and a 2026 trial in diabetes-free individuals with obesity and MASLD that examined adiposity.[16][17][18][19] Wikipedia observes that large high-quality studies are still needed and that berberine has frequently been withdrawn as a drug candidate.[1]

Gastrointestinal symptoms, notably constipation, diarrhea and flatulence, are the common side effects in trials and reviews.[1][3] Chinese labelling cautions against use in people with G6PD deficiency because of hemolytic anemia and jaundice, particularly in children.[1]

Berberine inhibits CYP3A4, and studies have shown that it can increase ciclosporin concentrations in kidney transplant recipients and midazolam concentrations in healthy volunteers.[1] Supplement quality varies: a 2017 study reported in Wikipedia found that only six of 15 products contained at least 90 percent of the labelled amount.[1] The FDA issued warning letters to eight manufacturers between 2020 and 2022 over false advertising and misbranded drug claims, and berberine is not generally recognised as safe (GRAS) in the United States.[1]

Laboratory work reported that berberine activates AMPK in cells and animals with metabolic benefit in diabetic and insulin-resistant states, and that it lowers cholesterol by a mechanism distinct from statins, increasing LDL receptor expression.[5][20] Other proposed actions include inhibition of pancreatic beta-cell potassium channels, glucose-dependent insulin secretion, and changes in the gut microbiota, which has been studied in rodents and in reviews.[2][21][22]

Oral bioavailability is low because of poor absorption and rapid metabolism, and some researchers propose that gut effects explain part of its activity. Registered trials have examined its absorption and sex differences in pharmacokinetics in healthy volunteers.[2][23][24]

Berberine has a tetracyclic skeleton biosynthesised from two L-tyrosine units, with a characteristic bridge carbon derived from an N-methyl group. It fluoresces yellow under ultraviolet light and has been used as a natural dye. On heating to 190 degrees Celsius it demethylates to berberrubine.[1]

Discussion is concentrated in strength-sport and bodybuilding forums rather than facial-aesthetics boards. Users compare it with metformin, mention a video on insulin, metformin and berberine for bodybuilding, and link a T Nation article on it, usually as a low-cost blood-sugar or partitioning aid.[12][13][14][25]

Nature Medicine paper describes cholesterol lowering by berberine through a mechanism distinct from statins.[20]

lore.intro: On strength and physique forums berberine is discussed as an inexpensive supplement for blood sugar, appetite and nutrient partitioning, often compared with metformin.[12][13][14]

claims.believers: Users note that it acts on AMPK like metformin and ask whether it can help with insulin sensitivity.[12][13]
claims.experts: Laboratory studies show AMPK activation, and a small 2008 trial found glucose-lowering similar to metformin in newly diagnosed diabetes; reviewers call for larger, higher-quality trials.[3][5][8]

claims.claim: It improves nutrient partitioning during a bulk
claims.believers: A T Nation poster lists berberine among methods for limiting fat gain while bulking.[14]
claims.experts: No published study has tested nutrient partitioning in lifters; meta-analyses concern glycemia and lipids in clinical populations.[3]

claims.claim: It reduces body weight and fat
claims.believers: Users take it during fat-loss phases for appetite and glucose control.[11][15]
claims.experts: A systematic review of weight-loss studies exists and the umbrella review lists body parameters among improved outcomes, but trials are small and uneven.[3][4]

claims.claim: It is a harmless natural supplement
claims.believers: Posters describe it as a natural option for people with a poor diet.[11]
claims.experts: Common gastrointestinal effects, CYP3A4 inhibition, G6PD cautions and FDA warning letters about marketing have been documented.[1][3]
